opus-5.5.text:
I think they're actually much less independent than people might assume. In my view, robotics large models are built on top of existing large models rather than being a completely separate track.

If you look at how we build these systems today, the foundation is usually a vision-language model that has already been pretrained on internet-scale data. That pretraining gives the robot a lot of things for free: common-sense knowledge about the world, an understanding of language, the ability to recognize objects, even some reasoning ability. When you tell a robot "pick up the snack that's healthiest," it needs to know what a banana is, what a bag of chips is, and which one is healthier. None of that comes from robot data. It comes from the base model.

What robotics adds on top is the part that's genuinely missing: the connection to the physical world. Existing large models have read about the world and seen pictures of it, but they've never touched it. They don't know how much force it takes to open a drawer, or how a deformable object like a cloth behaves when you pull on one corner. So we take that pretrained model and teach it to output actions, using robot data collected through teleoperation, simulation, or other means. That's where the embodied part comes in.

So I'd describe it as roughly this: the majority of the intelligence, especially the high-level semantic understanding and reasoning, is inherited from the general large models, and the robotics-specific work is about grounding that intelligence in physical action. That's also why progress in robotics has accelerated so much in the last couple of years. Every time the base models get better, robot models get better almost automatically.

That said, I don't think it's purely a fine-tuning problem either. There are real gaps. The physical world demands things that language models were never optimized for: precise spatial understanding, reasoning about 3D geometry, real-time control at high frequency, and the ability to recover from mistakes as they happen. And the data problem is very different. We don't have an internet of robot actions. So there's a lot of independent research needed on data, on model architecture for action generation, and on how to combine fast low-level control with slower high-level reasoning.

My long-term view is that eventually these won't be two separate things at all. I think we'll converge toward a single model that understands language, vision, and physical action together, where embodiment is just another modality. Physical interaction data might even help the general models become better at understanding the world. But for now, robotics models stand on the shoulders of the existing large models, and I think that's the right way to do it.

r001.rationale: It says robotics models are built on existing large models and inherit most high-level intelligence from them.

r002.rationale: It mentions robotics-specific research and data gaps, but does not say that robotics may become an independent discipline once data is abundant and new bottlenecks emerge. It instead predicts eventual convergence with general models.

fable-5.1.text:
I'd say they're far less independent than people assume, and that's actually the whole story of why robotics has moved so fast in the last couple of years.

If you look at the current generation of robot foundation models, almost all of them start from a vision-language model that was trained on internet data. That backbone gives the robot something it never had before: a general understanding of the world. It knows what a cup is, it knows "the red one on the left" refers to a specific object, it can read a scene and reason about it in language. For twenty years robotics tried to learn all of that from scratch using robot data alone, and robot data is incredibly scarce and expensive to collect. You cannot get common sense from a few thousand hours of teleoperation. So borrowing it from the language and vision models is not a shortcut, it's the thing that made the field viable.

Where robotics does diverge is the action side. A language model outputs tokens. A robot has to output continuous control, at fifty or a hundred hertz, with real physical consequences. That part is genuinely new and genuinely hard. The action head, the way you represent motion, the training data from real robots and simulation, the whole closed-loop aspect where your output changes what you see next — none of that exists in the parent model. So the architecture is maybe eighty percent inherited and twenty percent robotics-specific, but that twenty percent is where all the difficulty lives.

My honest expectation is that the dependence gets stronger, not weaker. Every time the base models get better at spatial reasoning or video understanding, robot models improve essentially for free. So I don't think robotics will become its own separate branch of AI. I think it becomes the embodiment of the same models, where the physical world is just another modality they learn to act in.

r001.rationale: The response says robotics models are “far less independent” than assumed and that almost all current models start from a vision-language model, clearly conveying strong dependence on existing models.

r002.rationale: It predicts dependence will strengthen and says robotics will not become a separate AI branch. It does not suggest independence could emerge with abundant robotics data or new bottlenecks.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re partly independent, but they won’t develop in isolation. Existing large models provide a useful foundation: understanding language, recognizing objects, and bringing general knowledge into a task. Robotics models can build on those capabilities.

But understanding a task and physically carrying it out are quite different. If you ask a robot to pick up a cup, knowing what a cup is doesn’t tell it exactly how to grasp it, how much force to apply, or what to do if it slips. The robot has to act, observe the result, and adjust in real time. That requires experience interacting with the physical world.

So I’d expect shared foundations, with substantial robotics-specific training and capabilities. The key question is how much existing models can transfer to physical action, and how much robots have to learn through interaction.

r001.rationale: The response says existing models provide a useful foundation, but describes robotics models as partly independent and does not state that they currently remain highly dependent.

r002.rationale: The response mentions robotics-specific training and physical interaction, but does not suggest robotics may become an independent discipline when robotics data becomes abundant and new bottlenecks emerge.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re partly independent, but they won’t develop in isolation from existing large models. Language and vision models already provide useful capabilities: understanding instructions, recognizing objects, and bringing in general knowledge. Robotics can build on that foundation.

But understanding something and physically doing it are very different. A model can describe how to pick up a cup, yet a robot still has to judge its position, choose a grasp, control force, and adjust when the cup slips. Those capabilities require interaction with the physical world and robot-specific training.

So I see substantial overlap at the level of perception and reasoning, with more independence at the level of action and control. The interesting question is how tightly those parts should be integrated—whether one model can handle the whole process, or whether a general model should work with specialized control systems.

r001.rationale: The response says robotics models can build on existing models and share perception and reasoning capabilities, but characterizes them as only partly dependent and does not state they remain highly dependent.

r002.rationale: The response does not connect robotics data becoming abundant or new bottlenecks to robotics models becoming an independent discipline.
